A question for U.S. interior design studios that work with remote designers: what are your biggest challenges when hiring international designers?

I’d genuinely love to hear from studio owners, principals, design directors, and hiring managers in the U.S.

As an interior designer working with U.S. projects, I’ve been thinking a lot about the gap between having the technical skills and actually being easy for a U.S. design studio to hire and work with remotely.

So I’d love to hear from the other side of the table:
When you consider hiring a remote/international interior designer, what are the biggest challenges or concerns you encounter?

For example:
• 🇺🇸 English & communication  Is language proficiency a major concern? Written communication? Meetings? Understanding design terminology?

• 📐 Portfolio What do you actually want to see? Beautiful renders? Technical drawings? Full project development? Before & after? Construction documents?

• 💻 Software & workflow  Which programs are essential for your studio? AutoCAD? SketchUp? Revit? Chief Architect? Adobe? AI tools?

• 📋 Technical knowledge  How important is knowledge of U.S. construction standards, detailing, millwork, lighting, electrical, materials, and specifications?

• 🏗️ Construction knowledge  Is understanding the U.S. construction process something you expect from a remote designer?

• 🎨 Design style Do you look for designers who already understand the American design aesthetic, or are technical skills and adaptability more important?

• ⏰ Time zones & availability  How much does working in a different time zone affect your decision?
• 🤝 Communication & collaboration What makes a remote designer easy—or difficultto work with?
• 💰 Payment & contracts  Does hiring someone internationally create concerns around payment methods, contracts, invoicing, taxes, or hourly vs. project-based work?

• 📁 Organization  How important are file organization, naming conventions, templates, project management, and documentation?

• 🤖 AI  Are you looking for designers who already know how to incorporate AI into their workflow?

• 🎯 Independence  Do you prefer someone who can execute very specific instructions, or someone who can take a project and run with it independently?

• 🌎 Understanding of the U.S. market  How important is it that an international designer understands U.S. suppliers, products, pricing, dimensions, and client expectations?
And most importantly:

What is something international designers often get wrong when trying to work with U.S. studios?

I’m asking because I believe the best way to become a better professional is to understand the real pain points on the other side of the hiring process.

So, U.S. designers and studio owners  what makes you say “YES, I want to work with this designer”... and what makes you hesitate?

I’d genuinely appreciate your perspective.

Feel free to comment honestly  I’m here to listen and learn. 🇺🇸🤝

💡Week4 Day5 - Understand DB tables - Coding create-payment in processsing-service

This week, I focused on payment database design and transaction processing, with an emphasis on traceability, data integrity, and clean separation of responsibilities.

The goal was to understand how payment information moves through the backend while remaining consistent and useful for troubleshooting and reconciliation.

 🔹 Designed payment master tables using primary and foreign keys to maintain relationships between payment data and provide a consistent source of truth.

 🔹 Structured payment records to retain merchant, internal, and payment-provider references, making it possible to trace a transaction across different systems.

 🔹 Implemented failure tracking by storing error codes, error messages, timestamps, and retry counts to support investigation and reconciliation of unsuccessful payments.

 🔹 Explored how detailed failure information can help understand what happened to a payment instead of relying only on its final status.

 🔹 Applied a layered processing flow where requests move through Controller → Service → Status Processor, keeping payment-processing responsibilities separated.

 🔹 Organized database operations behind dedicated Repository layers, keeping persistence concerns separate from payment-processing logic.

 🔹 Designed the transaction flow so that each layer has a focused responsibility, making the payment-processing code easier to understand and maintain.

 🔹 Built around a generic transaction DTO that carries the required payment information through different status processors without creating separate contracts for every status.

 🔹 Practiced using the same transaction data structure across status-processing logic, reducing unnecessary complexity while keeping the processors consistent.

 🔹 Connected database integrity, transaction traceability, failure tracking, layered processing, and a generic DTO into a practical payment backend design focused on maintainability and troubleshooting.

We have fewer people on our team than we did a year ago.

We also added 3 properties this year, with 3 more under contract. 

Most people hear "fewer people, more portfolio" and assume something went wrong. Nothing went wrong. One of our asset managers is moving to New York for a new chapter (excited for her, sad for us). When we sat down to backfill the role, we realized we did not need to replace her one for one.

Here is why. AI now handles the work that used to require a full seat: reporting, reconciliations, first-draft memos, routine coordination. And the honest truth is that work was never the actual job. It was the tax you paid to get to the part that mattered. What is left is the part that never gets automated. Walking a property. Reading a tenant. Catching the thing no report ever catches.

So we are hiring for a new seat: Property Operations Analyst. Half AI-fluent, half boots on the ground across our Bay Area portfolio.

If you want to learn real estate by doing it, not by watching it, this is the seat. 

We run this company on five values, and one of them is kaizen which is the focus on learning and continual improvement. We also shut the whole company down twice a year (Christmas and July 4). We also do an annual team trip to Mexico, where you have an outside shot at catching a marlin and a real shot at a terrible tequila hangover. We take our fun about as seriously as our underwriting.

The most overlooked shift in Data Governance for 2026 is not about policies, catalogs, or even AI compliance. It is the quiet transition from governance as a documentation exercise to governance as a real-time, machine-enforced trust signal that determines whether a query, a model, or a decision is allowed to execute at all.

The context confirms that automation and privacy-first design are becoming the norm. But the non-obvious consequence is that the traditional role of a data steward is being replaced by a new kind of role: the governance engineer. This person does not write policies for humans to read. They write machine-enforceable contracts that define the quality, provenance, and sensitivity of every dataset. They design the guardrails that prevent an AI agent from training on data with insufficient lineage, or a dashboard from surfacing metrics derived from stale sources.

The practical reality is that organizations are moving from a model where governance is a quarterly review with a compliance team to a model where governance is a runtime layer that evaluates every data access against a live set of constraints. This is not about locking data down. It is about creating a dynamic trust score that updates as data, models, and regulations change. A dataset that was trustworthy for reporting last week may no longer be suitable for an AI training pipeline today. The winning teams are the ones that have built the infrastructure to detect and enforce that difference in real time.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can write the most comprehensive governance framework. It is the one who can build the automated negotiation layer that makes governance a self-service trust signal rather than a centralized bottleneck. This requires a rare combination of distributed systems engineering, metadata architecture, and regulatory semantics. I specialize in this intersection. I design and implement governance-as-code systems that let data teams iterate at AI speed without compromising on trust or compliance.

The hardest problem right now is not the technology. It is the organizational shift from treating governance as a constraint to treating it as a decision-making accelerator. Teams that embed governance into the query layer and the CI/CD pipeline are winning. Teams that leave it as a spreadsheet are losing.

If your organization is scaling AI on regulated data, what is the one governance gap that a runtime trust score would solve faster than any policy manual ever could?

I've spent a little over $21K in the past five months trying almost every hiring, sourcing platform, ATS out there. 
I wanted one standard for my agency to build on top of. So that I don't experiment with different ones along the way.

I regret a lot, and I learned a lot. I just wish the lesson wasn't that expensive...

Most of them s&%k big time.

And yet I keep seeing stealth and early-stage startups with their career pages on these big ATSs.
Why? Why do you do that? You have 3 roles, 1-2 hires each... (once every half year)

If you're a small team planning 10, 15, 20 hires this year, you don't need a big, fancy, well-known ATS!
They're heavy. They're overkill and cumbersome.

Takes a lot of time to set up, even with their new AI features and MCP (all MCP's and API are very limiting by the way! you will still end up doing a lot manually, because of certain action is not in the API or MCP, that one you will have to do in the UI  🤦‍♂️ )

And they're expensive, much more than you think.
The price looks low at first.
It's per seat, per certain type of seat, and only one or two people use that type in the beginning.

Then you build a workflow that's actually transparent, fast, lean.
Hiring managers, interviewers, everyone in, with proper permissions.

But now everyone is a seat, because of that awesome workflow!
So next year when the contract renews, the bill multiplies. x20+

So you downgrade interviewers to lower permission roles so they don't count as seats.
Now the workflow isn't transparent or lean anymore. Your interviewers get a worse experience. So do your candidates...

You end up designing your hiring process around the pricing page!
And now can't see what's happening across roles and candidates without help anymore. 
You'll have to ask Claude to explain what is going on in your own ATS :D

Then what was the point of this overpriced ATS you chose, because of the clarity and transparency it seemed to provide? 

Switching hurts too. And the timing is never right

I believe most teams stay, eat the cost, and decide every ATS is the same.(after trying one or two)

I picked my one or two(depends on the needs). Not ideal. But pretty much great.
A huge save of cost and time.

Happy to share what I learned and help you set up something that makes sense.
And doesn't require a recruiter or TA like me to run it.

The $50,000 Hallucination.

Buying Copilot licenses for your accounting team is not an AI strategy. It is a software receipt.

Here is a pattern I keep seeing:

- A finance team connects an LLM to their data warehouse. 
- They ask it to explain a $50,000 revenue drop. 
- The model returns a polished, executive-ready explanation.

It is completely wrong.

The tool pulled from an unexecuted contract draft. It missed a pricing concession buried in a sales inbox. It ignored the company's own revenue recognition rules.

The team blamed the AI. But the model just did what probabilistic software does without context: it guessed.

The architecture failed. Not the prompt.

Before your finance function can safely use AI, four foundations have to be in place:
➡️ Data — one authoritative source per metric. If the CRM and ERP both have a "revenue" number, the model will pick the wrong one.

➡️ Context — executed contracts, side agreements, and accounting policies indexed and accessible. Not buried in email threads.

➡️ Intelligence — AI handles text: parsing, comparing, drafting. Deterministic systems handle the math. Never the other way around.

➡️ Governance — a controller reviews and signs off before anything reaches the ledger. The threshold, the approval chain, and the audit log are documented in writing.

Where to start? 
Pick one workflow — a variance explanation, a reconciliation exception, a contract comparison. 

Map it against the four foundations. 

Build it. 

Test it. 

Then scale.

So here's what I actually did to one of our blog pages this week.

Took "What Is Staff Augmentation," and rebuilt the whole thing around one question: if an AI model only lifted one sentence, would it pick the right one.
Four things changed.

Definition moved to sentence one. No warm-up, no "in today's competitive hiring market." Just: staff augmentation is a hiring model where external engineers join your in-house team on a flexible contract.

Added a sourced stat instead of a vague claim. "Many companies use external talent" became a specific number with a named source. Models want something they can quote and attribute, not a feeling.

Built a plain FAQ block. Short question, short answer. "Is staff augmentation the same as outsourcing?" No. Team extension where you direct the work, versus handing off an outcome entirely.

Swapped hedged phrasing for declarative sentences. "X is Y," not "X could be considered a form of Y." Clear definitions get lifted. Clever ones get skipped.
None of this is theory. It's just what I noticed after comparing pages that get cited against ones that don't.

Test everything, keep what works.
